rationale: Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-2: some households at the margin install because of the subsidy (the subsidy is about 18% of installed cost; surveys of intentions; payback periods).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-1: installers do not capture the whole subsidy (about 900 competing installers; subsidy shown on the invoice).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-2: more systems are installed because of the subsidy (C-2 rests on A-1 and A-2).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-4: installation labor cannot grow much within the first year (electrician licensing time, installer vacancies, backlog data).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-18: in the first year installers have clearly fewer alternatives than households, because their capacity is fixed by the number of licensed electricians while households can wait or keep buying grid power.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-5: certification is easy enough that new installers enter (a licensed electrician on staff, a three-day course and a $500 fee against the subsidy).

No matching assumption in WE-021; judged from the text: the text gives 900 MW as the funded total against about 105 MW a year before the policy, so over five years the cap binds only if installations run well above the old pace (about 180 MW a year, 1.7 times it); the subsidy cuts the cost by about 18%, which makes that possible but not likely.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-8: households knew of the subsidy from September and could wait (the bill was expected to pass; four months from introduction to effect).
Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-15: some adopters would have installed later without the subsidy (adoption trend; falling panel prices).

No matching assumption in WE-021; judged from the text: A-3 says demand changes little, not that it does not change; the surcharge is 0.12 cents on about 20 cents (0.6%), so the quantity falls at least a little, which is all the question asks. This is the premise of the wedge that carries the price rise.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-3: the surcharge is passed through to customers in full by Commission order (rates are set to recover costs through per-kWh charges).

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-3 read the other way: A-3 holds at 0.95 that the surcharge is passed through in full, and its 'if false' column says part falls on utilities, so utilities keeping part has the complement 0.05.

Probability taken from the assumption table of handbook WE-021 (illustrative figures), A-10: adopters buy less grid power after installing (rooftop output is an untaxed form of the taxed good, credited at the full retail rate).
No matching assumption in WE-021; judged from the text: retail electricity cannot be stored or ordered ahead by its buyers, so there is nothing to stockpile before the surcharge starts.
